glossary.definition: A private credential store per person, injected into that person's backend calls at request time, so the backend sees who actually acted instead of a shared service account. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

Every operation is forced to the calling user's own vault; there is no administrator override, and no admin, auditor or support role can read another user's credentials through the API. In the lab the caller is the only vault there is: no call takes an owner, another person's entry id is "not found", and naming an owner is refused. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

The MCP and agent-to-agent gateways, when an application is set to per-user credentials, build the credential from the caller's own entry and inject it into the backend call. The agent never holds it; the backend logs who actually acted. The gateway, agent and backend views are lab-invented simulations. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

Bearer tokens, API keys, username and password as HTTP Basic, and custom header pairs (slide 42). The exact wire form, header-name rules and field names are the lab's. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

AES-GCM with a unique nonce per value; the key is resolved at startup from AWS Secrets Manager with KMS envelope decryption or from HashiCorp Vault on premises, with a compiled-in development key only as fallback. The lab seals with real AES-256-GCM and a fresh 12-byte nonce per value, and binds the user id and entry id as additional authenticated data (lab-invented); the three key providers are mocks, and the development key is public on purpose. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

An update merges: omitting the secret keeps the stored value, so metadata can be edited without re-entering credentials. Merging field by field inside a credential is the lab's reading. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

A deletion is staged, then purged after 24 hours. In the lab it can be restored inside the window, is purged exactly at 24 hours (one minute short it is still there), and a staged entry cannot be edited or used. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

500 entries per user and 64 KB per credential, with entries whose target system is removed cleaned up automatically. The lab counts staged entries until they are purged and counts 64 KB as 65536 bytes over the secret fields; one byte over is refused whole. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

Discover and control the secrets already in AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, Delinea Secret Server and CyberArk PAM, preserving each store's structure, without becoming another copy of them. The five providers here are in-process mocks. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

The deck lists soft-delete and purge for Azure and file fields for Delinea. In the lab only Azure soft-deletes and purges; the other four delete permanently and refuse recover and purge (the lab's reading). Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

Rotation is triggered from Privilege for every provider. The lab replaces the password-type fields with a new labelled mock value, makes a new version and counts it. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

glossary.term: Read and write as separate grants
glossary.definition: Access runs through the same policy engine as the rest of the platform: read and write are separate grantable actions. The lab's grant shape (principal, "provider:path" scope, actions) is invented; a caller with no grant is told "not found", one holding only the other action is told "denied". Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.
Every secret read and mutation is audited, allowed or denied, with actor, role, action, resource and outcome. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

Only metadata (name, path, provider, tags and versions) is persisted; the value is excluded and fetched live from the provider at the moment of an authorized read. In the lab the value goes only into a simulated consumer, and a proof panel searches everything Privilege keeps for every value the providers hold (plain, base64, hex), with a planted-copy self-test. The method is lab-invented; provider credentials are sealed at rest. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

Connected stores re-synchronise nightly. The lab runs it when the lab clock crosses 02:00 and reports new, renamed, deleted and changed secrets from metadata only (rename found by the provider's own id); the time and finding kinds are lab-invented. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.
A clock the visitor advances (buttons for 1 minute, 1 hour, 23 hours 59 minutes, 24 hours and 1 day) so the 24-hour purge and the nightly re-sync can be seen. It only moves forward. Lab-invented.

cards.label: Scenario 1: Store a credential, edit it, use it
cards.description: A person stores a credential in their own vault, edits its notes without re-entering the secret, and the gateway uses it at request time. The backend logs who actually acted; with a shared service account it logs the same identity for everyone.

cards.label: Scenario 2: Delete, restore, then purge after 24 hours
cards.description: A deletion is staged, not immediate. It can be restored inside the window, and it is purged at exactly 24 hours: one minute short and it is still there.

cards.label: Scenario 3: Nobody else can read it, not even an administrator
cards.description: maya.chen has an entry. Another user, the administrator, the auditor and support each try to act on it, and each is forced into their own, empty, vault: not found. Naming an owner is refused.

cards.label: Scenario 4: Four credential shapes, injected at request time
cards.description: Bearer token, API key, HTTP Basic and a custom header pair: the gateway builds each from the caller's own entry, the agent sees none of it, and the backend identifies the caller from the credential. With no entry the call is refused: it does not fall back to a shared account.

cards.label: Scenario 5: Create, rotate, soft-delete and purge in a secret store
cards.description: In Azure Key Vault a secret gets created, rotated, soft-deleted, recovered, soft-deleted again and purged. Soft-delete and purge exist only where the deck lists them (Azure): AWS refuses. A Delinea secret with a file field is created too.

cards.label: Scenario 6: Read and write are separate grants
cards.description: The user can read an AWS secret but not rotate it; the administrator can rotate it but not read it. A value is delivered only to a simulated consumer, never into an API response. Everything is audited, allowed or denied.

cards.label: Scenario 7: The nightly re-sync notices what changed at the provider
cards.description: Someone renames one secret, deletes another and adds a third directly at the providers. Privilege is not told. When the lab clock crosses 02:00 the connected stores re-synchronise: metadata only, no value is ever requested.

cards.label: Try every other role
cards.description: Another user, the administrator, the auditor and support each ask for your entry: each is forced into their own empty vault.

cards.label: Call a backend with and without a shared account
cards.description: The gateway injects your credential; the agent sees nothing; the backend logs you. The shared account logs the same identity for everyone.

cards.label: Run the no-copy proof
cards.description: Search everything Privilege keeps for every value the providers hold; a planted copy proves the search works.

cards.label: Why it matters: User Vault (slide 42)
cards.description: Challenge: shared service accounts break attribution: every action looks the same in the target system's logs, and audit findings and access reviews on those accounts stall agent deployments that touch backends. Technical: each user's own credential injected at request time, so backends log who actually acted. Business: audit and access reviews on service accounts pass without backend changes, cutting compliance cost and review friction. These are Ping claims, unverified on our tenant.

cards.label: Why it matters: Secret Store Management (slide 43)
cards.description: Challenge: secrets sprawl across five secret managers with no unified view, policy or rotation, so governance effort grows and duplicates multiply storage and licence cost. Technical: one inventory and one request-approve policy across AWS, Google, Azure, Delinea and CyberArk, with no values ever stored. Business: eliminates duplicate-secret cost, reduces breach blast radius and standardizes rotation. These are Ping claims, unverified on our tenant.
